title: REST vs GraphQL Decision Framework
description: Apply a structured decision framework to choose between REST and GraphQL APIs for your C# services, based on client needs, data complexity, and operational constraints.

data.text: REST and GraphQL are both valid API styles, and neither is universally superior. REST is simple, cacheable, and widely understood. GraphQL is flexible, efficient for complex data graphs, and client-driven. The senior engineer's job is not to champion one over the other but to match the API style to the problem context: the client diversity, the data relationships, the caching requirements, and the team's operational maturity.

In a C# ecosystem, both styles are well-supported. REST is native to ASP.NET Core Minimal APIs and controllers. GraphQL is supported through Hot Chocolate, Strawberry Shake, and other mature libraries. The choice between them should be driven by requirements, not by familiarity or trend.

data.title: REST characteristics
items: Strengths: Simple to implement, leverages HTTP semantics and status codes, widely cached by CDNs and browsers, stateless and scalable.
Weaknesses: Over-fetching or under-fetching data is common, versioning strategies are inconsistent, multiple endpoints required for complex data graphs.

data.title: GraphQL characteristics
items: Strengths: Clients request exactly the data they need, single endpoint, strong type system, excellent for complex nested data.
Weaknesses: Query complexity can strain servers, caching is harder (no built-in HTTP caching), file uploads require workarounds, steeper learning curve for teams.

data.title: The N+1 problem in GraphQL
data.text: GraphQL's flexibility can create hidden performance problems. A single client query that requests nested lists can trigger dozens of database queries if the resolver is not optimized. In C#, use DataLoader patterns or compiled queries to batch and cache database calls within a single GraphQL request.

data.text: A minimal REST API in ASP.NET Core is concise and uses standard HTTP semantics. The client receives a fixed shape of data, which is predictable and easy to cache.

data.title: Minimal REST API for orders
data.content: A REST endpoint returning a fixed data shape with standard HTTP status codes.

data.text: With Hot Chocolate, a GraphQL resolver can return nested data in a single request. The client controls the shape of the response, which eliminates over-fetching but requires careful attention to resolver performance.

data.content: A GraphQL query type that resolves orders with nested customer and item data.

data.text: REST and GraphQL are not mutually exclusive. Many organizations run both: REST for simple, public-facing endpoints and GraphQL for internal or mobile APIs that need flexible data access. In a C# solution, you can host both in the same ASP.NET Core application using separate route prefixes. The key is to apply each style where it provides the most value.

data.title: Choose an API style for a new feature
data.description: Evaluate REST and GraphQL for a specific feature in your current or imagined project.
steps: Define a feature that needs an API: product catalog, dashboard analytics, or social feed.
List the clients that will consume the API: web, mobile, third-party.
Assess the data relationships: flat, moderately nested, or deeply interconnected.
Evaluate caching requirements: is HTTP caching important, or is fine-grained client caching acceptable?
Choose REST or GraphQL and write a one-paragraph justification using the decision framework.
Sketch the first query or endpoint and identify the main performance risk.
data.expectedOutcome: A justified API style choice with a sketch of the first endpoint or query and an identified risk.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: REST is simpler, more cacheable, and better for well-known clients with simple data needs.
GraphQL is more flexible for complex data graphs but requires careful resolver optimization.
Use a decision framework based on client diversity, data relationships, caching, and team maturity.
REST and GraphQL can coexist in the same application when each serves its strengths.
data.takeaway: API style is an architecture decision, not a default. Senior engineers choose REST or GraphQL based on the specific problem context, not on hype or familiarity.
